name: 22q11.2 microduplication syndrome
aliases: reciprocal duplication of the DiGeorge/velocardiofacial region

reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Represents the reciprocal rearrangement of the interval lost in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, arising through the same low-copy-repeat mechanism
The phenotype is strikingly variable, spanning apparently unaffected carriers through to individuals with intellectual disability
Common findings include developmental delay, learning difficulty, hypotonia and delayed speech
Growth restriction and mild, often subtle, facial dysmorphism may be present but are inconsistent
Frequently inherited from a parent who is healthy or only minimally affected, underscoring incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity
Congenital heart disease and palatal anomalies can occur but are generally milder and less frequent than in the reciprocal deletion
The finding is often incidental on chromosomal microarray requested for developmental delay or autistic features
Because many carriers are well, careful counselling about the uncertain outlook is central to management
reference.pathophysiology: The 22q11.2 region is flanked by blocks of segmental duplication (low-copy repeats) that misalign during meiosis and predispose to non-allelic homologous recombination. This process can generate either a deletion or the reciprocal duplication of the intervening dosage-sensitive segment, which harbours numerous genes including TBX1. Gain of an extra copy of this interval perturbs early pharyngeal and neurodevelopmental pathways, but the phenotypic effect of the gain is far less consistent than that of the loss. The wide variability and reduced penetrance are incompletely understood and probably reflect additional genetic background and environmental modifiers.
additionalDifferentials: Other recurrent copy-number syndromes causing developmental delay, such as 16p11.2 or 1q21.1 rearrangements
additionalInvestigations: Chromosomal microarray as the first-line test to detect the copy-number gain and define its extent
FISH or MLPA to confirm the duplication and characterise the breakpoints
Parental testing to establish whether the change is inherited or de novo and to guide recurrence-risk counselling
Echocardiography to screen for structural congenital heart disease
Cognitive and autism evaluation where the history warrants it
redFlags: Structural congenital heart disease requiring cardiology input
Palatal insufficiency causing feeding difficulty or hypernasal speech
Unexpected developmental regression prompting broader reassessment
Recurrent infection raising concern about immune involvement
reference.prognosis: The outlook is highly variable and often favourable: many carriers have normal or near-normal function, while others have mild to moderate learning and developmental difficulties that benefit from early support. Serious organ malformation is uncommon, so long-term prognosis usually depends on the degree of neurodevelopmental involvement rather than on medical complications.
pitfalls: Assuming a duplication is benign simply because an apparently healthy parent also carries it, given the marked variable expressivity
Over-interpreting the finding as a complete explanation for a child's difficulties and missing coexisting conditions
Failing to offer cardiac and palatal assessment because the change is regarded as mild
Providing overly definitive prognostic statements despite the uncertain natural history
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Provide developmental and educational support with speech-and-language therapy for delayed speech and learning difficulty
Offer physiotherapy and occupational therapy for hypotonia and motor delay
Screen for structural congenital heart disease with echocardiography and manage any defect, which is generally milder than in the reciprocal deletion
Assess and manage palatal anomalies with speech-and-language and ENT input where feeding or speech is affected
Undertake cognitive and autism evaluation where the history warrants and provide tailored support
Offer genetic counselling with parental testing, recognising the duplication is frequently inherited, and counsel recurrence risk
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary developmental and genetics team
